title: CS103 Unit 0 - Course Intro
summary: Title slide introducing the CS103 Introduction to Programming course, taught by Mark Redekopp.
main_text: CS103 Unit 0 - Course Intro. Instructor: Mark Redekopp. This is the opening title slide for the course introduction unit of CS103, Introduction to Programming.
notes_text: First slide of the deck; establishes course and unit identity for CS103.

title: Welcome to Computer Science
summary: Visual collage showcasing diverse applications of computer science including AI, autonomous vehicles, robotics, VR, smartphones, and DNA analysis.
main_text: Welcome to Computer Science. This slide presents a visual overview of the many exciting fields and applications powered by computer science. Images include an AI brain circuit, autonomous vehicles communicating on a road, a smartphone with various app icons, a VR headset, a humanoid robot, a DNA double helix figure, and a robotic prosthetic hand shaking a human hand. These images collectively illustrate the breadth of computer science applications across artificial intelligence, autonomous driving, mobile computing, virtual reality, robotics, bioinformatics, and assistive technology.
notes_text: Motivational opening slide. Establishes that CS is not just about writing code but touches virtually every modern technology domain.

images.description: AI brain made of circuit patterns, glowing blue, teaching that AI involves computational neural structures
Autonomous vehicles on a road with wireless communication signals between them, illustrating self-driving car technology
Smartphone screen showing colorful app icons representing mobile computing
White VR headset illustrating virtual reality technology
DNA double helix figure made of dots showing bioinformatics applications
Humanoid robot in mid-air pose demonstrating advanced robotics
Robotic prosthetic hand grasping a human hand, showing assistive technology

title: What is Computer Science
summary: Defines computer science as interdisciplinary problem-solving using algorithms, not just about computers themselves.
main_text: If someone asks, 'What is computer science?', we might answer, 'All science is computer science!' It is very interdisciplinary: Math, Engineering, Medicine, Natural sciences, Art, Linguistics, Social Sciences etc. It is more about problem-solving and developing algorithms to solve information-based problems. Example problems include: How do I recognize objects in a photograph or video? What patterns can be found in a set of data that would allow me to predict future outcomes? Identify the function of this protein given its structure.
notes_text: Key takeaway: CS is fundamentally about algorithms and problem-solving across disciplines, not just about the machines. The examples span computer vision, data science/machine learning, and bioinformatics.

title: What Computer Scientists Do
summary: Computer scientists find algorithmic methods for information problems and convert them into executable programs; the course covers both.
main_text: What Computer Scientists Do: Find methods to solve information-based problems (algorithms) -- this is truly CS. Observe, organize, transform and discover useful information from data. Use math and logic to solve problems. Work in cross-discipline groups. Convert these methods/algorithms to a form that a computer can execute -- this is programming. Computer science is no more about computers than astronomy is about telescopes. Computers are the primary tool. We generally do both algorithm design and programming. The famous quote about telescopes emphasizes that CS focuses on the science of computation, not just the hardware.
notes_text: Distinguishes the two core activities: algorithm design (the intellectual core) and programming (the practical implementation). The telescope analogy is attributed to Edsger Dijkstra, though the slide notes the attribution is unclear.

title: Computer Science Is a Great Career Path
summary: Computer science is a great way to make a living; Maria Klawe argues that CS and engineering lead to solving the world's biggest challenges.
main_text: Computer Science Is a great way to make a living. Maria Klawe, et. al. states: To the age-old question -- 'What do you want to do when you grow up?' -- children today give many modern answers: 'Help feed hungry families.' 'Prevent and cure diseases.' 'Find sources of renewable energy.' 'Understand the universe.' One clear path leads to each of these aspirations: the study of computer science (and engineering).
notes_text: Motivational slide using a quote from Maria Klawe (former president of Harvey Mudd College) to illustrate how computer science is central to addressing major societal challenges from hunger to healthcare to energy.

title: CS 103 or CS 102
summary: CS103 is Introduction to Programming requiring prior experience; CS102 is a slower-paced alternative. CS103 uses C/C++ and teaches efficient coding.
main_text: CS103: Introduction to Programming. It is an introduction but requires some prior programming experience. Students must have passed the AP CS exam and/or the CS 102 placement exam. Should know one of Java or C/C++. Those that meet the above criteria but don't feel confident may consider CS 102 as a slower-paced on ramp to programming. Programming: The course will try to teach good coding practices and how to find efficient solutions (not just any solution). The course will focus on concepts present in most languages using C/C++ as the primary language (not Java nor Python).
notes_text: Important course placement information. CS103 assumes students already have basic programming skills from AP CS or equivalent. The focus on C/C++ is deliberate because it teaches concepts transferable to other languages.

images.description: Two photos of highway interchanges/roads, metaphorically representing the two paths (CS102 vs CS103) students can take

title: Course Structure
summary: CS103 has 6 units, each with lectures, labs, homework, and projects covering C++ Bootcamp through Recursion.
main_text: The course is broken into 6 units each consisting of: Lectures, Labs (Tools + Practice + small group help), Homework(s) (Formative programming problems), and Project(s) (Cumulative programming problems). The 6 units are: Unit 1 - C++ Bootcamp, Unit 2 - Pointers and Memory, Unit 3 - Objects 1, Unit 4 - Managing Data, Unit 5 - Objects 2, Unit 6 - Recursion.
notes_text: Overview of the entire course structure. Each unit follows a consistent pattern of lectures for theory, labs for hands-on practice with TA support, homework for formative assessment, and projects for cumulative problem-solving. The progression goes from C++ basics through advanced topics like pointers, OOP, data management, and recursion.

images.description: Diagram showing unit structure with icons for Lectures (podium), Labs (tools), Homework (house), and Projects (laptop), plus numbered circles 1-6 for each unit topic

title: Exams and Grading
summary: Grading uses a points-based system starting at C (2 points), with additive/subtractive points from labs, HW, projects, midterms, and final totaling 8 for an A.
main_text: The grading system uses a cumulative point scale: A=8, A-=7, B+=6, B=5, B-=4, C+=3, C=2, D=1, F=0. Students start at C (2 points). Lab: +1 (Miss at most 3 labs), +0 otherwise. HW (Late work: Max 75%): +1 (Earn 75% or more on each), +0 otherwise. Projects (Late work: Max 75%): +1 (Earn >=75 on 2; 100 on all others), +0 (Earn >=50 on 1, >=75 on 2, and 100 on all others), -1 otherwise. Written MT (WMT): +1 (80-100), +0 (60-79), -1 (<60). Programming MT (PMT): +1 (80-100), +0 (<80). Final: +1 (80-100), +0 (60-79), -1 (<60). Total of 8 points equals an A.
notes_text: Unique grading system that works additively from a C baseline. Students earn or lose points in each category rather than having weighted percentage grades. This incentivizes consistent performance across all categories rather than compensating weakness in one area with strength in another.

images.description: Grade scale table on the left showing letter grades from A (8) to F (0) with color coding, and a criteria table on the right showing point values for each category

title: Syllabus
summary: Section divider slide indicating the syllabus section of the course introduction.
main_text: Syllabus. This is a section divider slide directing students to review the course syllabus.
notes_text: Transition slide. Students should refer to the actual syllabus document for full details on course policies.

title: Academic Integrity
summary: Emphasizes academic integrity policies: violations prevent dropping the class, plagiarism detection tools are used, and relying on others or AI undermines skill building.
main_text: Be sure you re-read the academic integrity guidelines on the syllabus. If you have a violation, you cannot drop the class! The goal is for you to build the programming 'muscles' you need to excel in future courses and your career. And you can't do that if you rely too heavily on someone else or AI. We run tools that check every submission against every other. The slide shows a plagiarism detection tool output ranking submissions by similarity, with code comparison examples showing suspiciously similar code between different submissions.
notes_text: Strong warning about academic dishonesty. The course uses automated code similarity detection tools (like MOSS or similar) that rank and compare all student submissions. The visual evidence of detected plagiarism serves as a deterrent.

images.description: Screenshot of plagiarism detection tool showing ranked submissions with similarity percentages and side-by-side code comparison of two suspicious submissions

title: Expectations
summary: Students should attend lectures, engage actively, start assignments early, study after each lecture, and seek full understanding.
main_text: Attend lectures and be engaged. Ask questions. We're a team... I need you! I'll give you my best. Try to give me yours! Catch the wave! Start assignments early, complete them early. Study and review after each lecture. Read more on your own or ask questions and don't be satisfied with partial understanding.
notes_text: Sets the tone for student engagement. The 'catch the wave' metaphor (illustrated by a surfer photo) emphasizes that falling behind in a programming course creates compounding difficulty, so staying current with material is essential.

images.description: Photo of a surfer riding a wave, metaphorically representing 'catching the wave' of staying on top of coursework

main_text: Teaching faculty in EE and CS. Undergrad at USC in CECS. Grad at USC in CEng. Worked at Raytheon. Sports enthusiast! Watching: All sports. Playing: Basketball, Baseball, Ultimate Frisbee, Pickleball. Enjoys languages (other than programming languages): Spanish and some Chinese.
notes_text: Personal introduction from the instructor to build rapport with students. Establishes credibility through industry experience at Raytheon and USC education background.

images.description: Professional headshot photo of Mark Redekopp, the course instructor

title: Programming Languages and C++ - Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing the topic of programming languages and C++.
main_text: Programming Languages and C++. This is a section divider slide transitioning to the topic of programming languages with a focus on C++.
notes_text: Marks the transition from course logistics to technical content about programming languages and why C++ is used in this course.

title: Programming Languages
summary: Imperative languages require focus on both data and algorithms; programming is like cooking with ingredients (data) and recipes (algorithms).
main_text: Programming in imperative (or 'structured') languages (like C++, Java, Python) requires you to focus on both the what (the data) and the how (the algorithm). It is like being a cook. The quality of the dish depends on the ingredients (the data) and the recipe (the algorithm). But you have to come up with the recipe yourself, though we'll give you some techniques so that you understand what options you have and what might work well. But it's up to you to put them together (i.e. make it delicious)! The slide shows a Python quadratic equation solver code example alongside a cooking analogy diagram showing that a computer reads instructions and operates on data, just as a cook follows a recipe using ingredients.
notes_text: The cooking analogy is a powerful way to understand the dual nature of programming: data (ingredients) must be combined using algorithms (recipes). The quadratic formula solver is a concrete example of both -- the coefficients a, b, c are data, and the formula is the algorithm.

images.description: Side-by-side comparison: Python code for a quadratic equation solver on the left, and a cooking analogy diagram on the right showing instructions (recipe) and data (flour, eggs) feeding into a computer/cook

title: Why C/C++
summary: C/C++ is taught because it is popular, ubiquitous, close to hardware, and learning it enables quickly picking up other languages.
main_text: We will teach C++ in this course because: C/C++ is still a very popular language in industry. C/C++ is ubiquitous -- used everywhere, even to implement other programming languages (i.e. Python, Matlab, etc.). C/C++ is close to the actual hardware. This makes it fast and flexible (near direct control of the hardware). This also makes it dangerous (near direct control of the hardware). It is most common in embedded devices (your phone, car, wireless router, etc.). Principles and concepts of C/C++ will allow you to quickly learn other programming languages. C/C++ is extremely broad and allows you to learn other languages easily. Not Java.
notes_text: The dual nature of C/C++ being both powerful and dangerous is a recurring theme throughout CS103. Being close to hardware means direct memory manipulation, which enables performance but also creates risks like buffer overflows and memory leaks -- topics covered later in the course.

title: History of C and C++
summary: Timeline of C/C++ evolution from Algol (1960) through BCPL, B, C, K&R C, to C++ (1980) by Bjarne Stroustrup and modern ISO standards.
main_text: History of C and C++: Algol was created by an international group in 1960. Basic Combined Programming Language (BCPL) was created by Martin Richards in 1967. B was created by Ken Thompson in 1970. C was created by Dennis Ritchie in 1972. K&R C was defined by Brian Kernighan and Dennis Ritchie in 1978. C++ was created by Bjarne Stroustrup in 1980. C++-98 and 03 were ISO/IEC 14882:1998/2003 standards from 1998 and 2003. C++-11,14,17,20 are ISO/IEC 14882:2011 standards from 2011 and onward.
notes_text: Shows the evolutionary chain of programming languages leading to C++. Each language built upon its predecessor. Bjarne Stroustrup (shown in the photo) created C++ as an extension of C to add object-oriented features while maintaining C's low-level capabilities.

images.description: Table showing the chronological evolution of C-family languages from Algol (1960) to modern C++ standards, with a photo of Bjarne Stroustrup and an arrow highlighting C++'s creation

title: Philosophy of C++
summary: C++ philosophy emphasizes C compatibility, programmer choice and efficiency, and minimalism -- the language forces nothing extra upon you.
main_text: Philosophy of C++: Compatibility -- The language should be compatible with C. The transition from C to C++ should not be difficult (yeah right!). Choice (and Efficiency) -- The language should give the option to programmers to make their own choice, even if it increases the possibility that a programmer will choose incorrectly. The language should not slow down a program or consume space (overhead) for the features not used in the code. Summary: Minimalist. C and C++ force nothing extra upon you (even protections). If you want 'extra', implement it yourself or use a library. From 'The Design and Evolution of C++' by Bjarne Stroustrup.
notes_text: This minimalist philosophy is why C++ can be dangerous: it does not provide safety nets like automatic bounds checking or garbage collection. This gives maximum performance and control but places the burden of correctness on the programmer. This is a fundamental design tradeoff students must understand.

images.description: Photo of a scenic road with fall foliage and a 'no' prohibition sign, metaphorically illustrating that C++ does not restrict the programmer's path

title: Fact 1 and Fact 2 - Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing two fundamental facts about computers that students should always remember.
main_text: Two facts to always remember. Fact 1 and Fact 2. This is a section divider introducing two foundational concepts about how computers process information.
notes_text: Transition slide setting up the two most important conceptual takeaways of Unit 0: everything is a number, and computers operate on only 1 or 2 numbers at a time.

images.description: Cartoon illustration of Thing 1 and Thing 2 characters from Dr. Seuss, playfully representing the two facts

title: It's A Numbers Game
summary: Two fundamental facts: everything in a computer is a number, and computer operations can only operate on 1 or 2 numbers at a time.
main_text: Fact 1: Everything in a computer is a number. Sure, things like 103 and 3.9 are numbers. But what about text and images and sound? Everything! Fact 2: Computer operations can only operate on 1 or 2 numbers at a time. Humans process information differently. Therein lies some of the difficulty of learning programming. The slide shows a Python quadratic equation solver and a recipe card to illustrate that both code instructions and data are ultimately represented as numbers.
notes_text: These two facts are the foundational mental model for the entire course. Fact 1 explains why we need encoding schemes (ASCII for text, pixel values for images, etc.). Fact 2 explains why complex operations require loops and iteration -- the computer cannot process an entire string or array at once, only one element at a time.

images.description: Python code for quadratic equation solver alongside a recipe card diagram, showing that programs consist of instructions operating on data, all represented as numbers

title: Example 1 - Character as Number
summary: Demonstrates Fact 1: humans see the letter 'a', but the computer sees the number 97 -- each text character is coded to a number.
main_text: What do you see? The letter 'a'! What does the computer see? A number: each text character is coded to a number. Example: Character map / Insert symbol. The letter 'a' is displayed as a large character on the right, with the number 97 shown below it, demonstrating that what humans perceive as a letter is stored as an integer value by the computer.
notes_text: This is the first concrete example of Fact 1. The number 97 is the ASCII code for lowercase 'a'. This mapping between characters and numbers is how all text is stored and processed in computers.

title: Text Representation - ASCII Table
summary: ASCII (UTF-8) is the most common character encoding; every character including non-printing ones has a decimal and hexadecimal number.
main_text: Most common character code is ASCII (UTF-8). Every character, even non-printing characters, have a corresponding number. Numbers are represented in Decimal (base 10) and Hexadecimal (base 16). The slide displays a complete ASCII chart showing the mapping between decimal values, hexadecimal values, and characters. Notable mappings highlighted include: 'A' = 65 (decimal) = 41 (hex), 'a' = 97 (decimal) = 61 (hex). The table includes control characters (0-31), printable characters (32-126), and extended characters.
notes_text: The ASCII table is a fundamental reference for understanding text processing in C/C++. Students should note that uppercase and lowercase letters differ by 32 (a consistent offset), which enables easy case conversion. The hex representation becomes important when examining memory contents.

images.description: Complete ASCII chart table showing decimal value, hexadecimal value, character name, and control character mappings, with 'A'=65 and 'a'=97 highlighted in red boxes

title: Example 2 - Image as Numbers
summary: Humans see a face in an image, but the computer sees individual pixel values representing shades of gray or color.
main_text: What do you see? A face! What does the computer see? Individual pixels whose value indicates the shade of gray (or color). The slide shows a grayscale photograph of a man's face. A zoomed-in section reveals the individual pixels, which are then mapped to a grid of numerical values: 0 (black), 64, 128, 192 (varying shades of gray). Each pixel is represented by a number where 0 is black and higher values approach white.
notes_text: Second example of Fact 1 applied to images. Each pixel in a digital image is just a number. In grayscale, 0=black and 255=white. In color images, each pixel has multiple numbers (e.g., RGB values). This numerical representation is what enables computational image processing.

images.description: Grayscale portrait photo with a zoomed-in circle showing individual pixels, which are then mapped to a 4x4 grid of numerical values (0, 64, 128, 192) representing gray levels

title: The Connection with Mathematics - Brightness and Contrast
summary: Image brightness and contrast adjustments are mathematical operations on pixel values: addition for brightness, multiplication for contrast.
main_text: Brightness: Each pixel value is increased/decreased by a constant amount. P_new = P_old + B. B > 0 = brighter, B < 0 = less bright. Contrast: Each pixel value is multiplied by a constant amount. P_new = C * P_old + k. C > 1 = more contrast, 0 < C < 1 = less contrast. Same operations performed on all pixels. The slide shows the original grayscale portrait with variants showing increased/decreased brightness and increased/decreased contrast, along with a graph showing the input pixel to output pixel mapping.
notes_text: This demonstrates how simple mathematical operations (addition and multiplication) applied to numbers (pixel values) produce meaningful visual effects. This is a concrete example of why Fact 1 (everything is a number) matters: once data is numerical, math can transform it.

images.description: Grid of five versions of the same portrait showing effects of brightness and contrast adjustments, with a transfer function graph showing input vs output pixel values

title: But Why - Why Computers Process One Value at a Time
summary: Computers store pixel values as separate numbers in RAM and the processor must retrieve them one at a time via the memory bus.
main_text: Why can't a computer just 'look' at the image? Computers store information as numbers (e.g., each pixel of an image is a separate number). These numbers are stored as units of 8-, 32- or 64-bits in the computer's RAM (memory). The computer processor must retrieve them from memory 1 at a time. The slide shows the same portrait-to-pixel-grid transformation from earlier, plus a diagram showing an Intel Core i7 processor connected to a RAM module with a bidirectional arrow labeled 'Can only transfer 1 value at a time'.
notes_text: This slide bridges Fact 1 and Fact 2. Because images are stored as many individual numbers in memory, and the processor can only fetch one value at a time, processing an image requires iterating through every pixel -- hence the need for loops in programming.

images.description: Diagram showing an Intel Core i7 processor chip connected to a RAM memory stick with a bidirectional arrow, labeled 'Can only transfer 1 value at a time', alongside the portrait-to-pixel-grid example
labels: Can only transfer 1 value at a time

title: Memory Operations - Read and Write
summary: RAM is a set of addressable cells; the processor reads or writes one location at a time using address, data, and control signals.
main_text: Memory (RAM) is a set of cells that each store a group of bits (usually, 1 byte = 8 bits). Each cell is referenced via a unique address. Processor can access 1 location at a time, either reading or writing that location. Read: retrieves data value in a particular location (specified using the address). Write: changes data in a location to a new value. The slide shows two diagrams: A Read Operation where the processor sends address 2 (00000010) and control signal Read (1), and receives data 0 (00000000) from memory address 2. A Write Operation where the processor sends address 2 (00000010), data 192 (11000000), and control signal Write (0) to store the new value.
notes_text: This is the hardware foundation for understanding variables in programming. When you write 'x = 5' in C++, the computer is performing a Write operation to a specific memory address. When you read 'y = x', it performs a Read to retrieve the value. Understanding this hardware model helps explain pointers and references later in the course.

images.description: Two diagrams showing processor-memory interaction: Read operation (processor sends address 2, gets data 0) and Write operation (processor sends address 2 with data 192), with memory shown as numbered cells containing binary values

title: 1 or Many - Section Divider
summary: Section divider posing the question: do code tasks require 1 operation or many operations?
main_text: Do the following code tasks require 1 operation or many? This section divider introduces exercises that help students develop intuition about which programming operations are simple (single) and which require multiple steps behind the scenes.
notes_text: This section builds directly on Fact 2 (computers operate on 1 or 2 numbers at a time) by having students analyze code to determine operation complexity.

title: One Operation or Many (1) - Question
summary: Asks whether assigning int vs string variables requires one or many operations, showing side-by-side C++ code examples.
main_text: Do the following require a 1-to-1 operation (adding, comparing, or changing single numbers) or many-to-many? Left example: int x = 1, y = 2; x = y; -- One / Many? Right example: string x = "abc", y = "defg"; x = y; -- One / Many? The two code examples are shown side by side in yellow-highlighted code boxes, both using #include <iostream>, #include <string>, and using namespace std.
notes_text: This is a think-pair-share exercise. Students should reason about what happens at the hardware level for each assignment. Integer assignment moves a single number. String assignment must copy multiple characters one at a time.

images.description: Two side-by-side yellow code boxes showing C++ programs: left with int variables, right with string variables, each asking whether x = y is one or many operations

title: One Operation or Many (1) - Answer
summary: Integer assignment is one operation; string assignment is many operations because strings are composite objects (arrays) to a computer.
main_text: Left example with int: One operation. Right example with string: Many operations. Key insight: ints are single objects to a computer. strings are composite objects (i.e. an array) to a computer. The same code examples are repeated with the answers revealed: integer assignment is a single operation because an int is one number, while string assignment requires many operations because a string is an array of characters that must be copied one at a time.
notes_text: This is the core lesson: what looks like a simple operation in high-level code may require many low-level operations. The distinction between primitive types (int, char, double) and composite types (string, vector, array) is fundamental to understanding performance and memory management in C++.

images.description: Same two code boxes with answers revealed: 'One' under the int example and 'Many' under the string example, with an explanatory note box

title: Strings Overview
summary: Strings abstract character arrays; behind the scenes they manage dynamic memory allocation, copying old contents when the array grows too large.
main_text: strings simply abstract character arrays. Behind the scenes strings are just creating and manipulating character arrays but giving you a simplified set of operators and functions. When the contents of the string grow too large, a new array is allocated behind the scenes (potentially copying the contents of the old string). Example code: string str2 = "abc"; stores 3 characters. int y = 5; is stored at a single location. str2 = "defgh"; now stores 5 characters, requiring a new allocation. The memory diagram shows str2's internal structure with a size field (5) and a pointer to address 2812 where the characters 'd','e','f','g','h','\0' are stored as binary values in consecutive memory locations.
notes_text: This slide previews how strings work internally, which will be covered in depth during the pointers and memory unit. The key insight is that a string variable is not just a simple value but a complex object managing a pointer to a dynamically allocated character array, a size, and potentially a capacity.

images.description: Memory diagram showing a string object str2 containing a pointer to address 2812, size 5, and the character array at memory addresses 2812-2817 storing 'd','e','f','g','h','\0' in binary

title: One Operation or Many (2) - Question
summary: Asks whether comparing char variables vs string variables requires one or many operations.
main_text: Left example: char c = 'a', d = 'b'; if(c == d) { ... } -- One / Many? Right example: string x = "abc", y = "acb"; if(x == y) { ... } -- One / Many? Two C++ code examples are shown side by side, both checking equality but with different data types: char (single character) vs string (multiple characters).
notes_text: Builds on the previous exercise but now with comparison operations instead of assignment. Students should apply the same reasoning: how many individual values need to be compared?

images.description: Two side-by-side yellow code boxes: left comparing char variables c and d, right comparing string variables x and y, each asking One / Many

title: One Operation or Many (2) - Answer
summary: Comparing chars is one operation; comparing strings is many because each character must be compared individually element by element.
main_text: Left example with char: One operation. Right example with string: Many operations. chars, doubles, ints can be compared in a single operation. strings are arrays and must be compared character by character. The answer diagram shows char c stored at memory location 12 with value 'a', and char d at location 18 with value 'b' -- comparing these is one operation. For strings, x is stored as array ['a','b','c','\0'] at locations 20-22, and y as ['a','c','b','\0'] at locations 34-36 -- comparing these requires checking each character position sequentially.
notes_text: Reinforces the distinction between primitive and composite types for comparison operations. String comparison in C++ uses the == operator which abstracts the character-by-character loop, but behind the scenes it must iterate through each character until a mismatch is found or all characters match.

images.description: Memory layout diagrams showing char variables c and d as single memory cells, and string arrays x and y as sequences of characters in memory, with answers 'One' and 'Many'

title: One Operation or Many (3) - Vector push_back
summary: Asks whether appending to a vector with push_back requires one or many operations; shows vector array indices before and after.
main_text: Code example: vector<int> y = {1,2,3}; y.push_back(4); // append 1 int. One / Many? The slide shows the vector y initially containing elements [1, 2, 3] at indices 0, 1, 2. After push_back(4), the vector contains [1, 2, 3, 4] at indices 0, 1, 2, 3.
notes_text: This exercise introduces vectors and the push_back operation. The answer depends on whether the vector needs to resize: if there is capacity, it is one operation (store the value and increment size). If the vector must resize, it requires many operations (allocate new array, copy all old elements, store new element).

images.description: Yellow code box showing vector initialization and push_back, with array diagrams showing the vector before (3 elements) and after (4 elements) the push_back call

title: What Happens Behind the Scenes - Vector Resize
summary: Vectors abstract arrays; push_back may trigger reallocation when capacity is exceeded, requiring copying all old contents to a larger array.
main_text: Vectors abstract arrays. Behind the scenes vectors are just creating and manipulating arrays but giving you a simplified set of operators and functions. Example code creates vector<int> v1(5) and fills it with values 50-54 using a for loop, then calls v1.push_back(10) which causes a resize behind the scenes. The internal structure shows v1 with data pointer, capacity (cap=10), and size (6). Initially the array has 5 elements [50,51,52,53,54] with capacity 5. After push_back(10), a new larger array is allocated with capacity 10, old values are copied, and 10 is added at index 5, giving [50,51,52,53,54,10,?,?,?,?]. Growing an array (which is the underlying structure of a vector) may require reallocating a larger array and copying the old contents.
notes_text: This is a preview of the Pointers and Memory unit (Unit 2). The vector's internal structure (data pointer, size, capacity) is similar to the string's internal structure shown earlier. The reallocation cost is why vectors typically double their capacity -- amortizing the copy cost over many push_back operations.

images.description: Diagram showing vector v1's internal structure (data pointer, cap=10, size=6) and the array before and after resize, with old 5-element array pointing to new 10-element array

title: Think Like a Computer - Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing exercises about thinking like a computer that can only process 1 or 2 values at a time.
main_text: Fact 2: A computer operation can only process 1 or 2 values at a time. Think Like a Computer. This section introduces exercises that challenge students to solve problems the way a computer would -- processing only one or two data items at each step.
notes_text: Transition to the path planning exercise which serves as an extended example of thinking algorithmically with the constraint that you can only examine limited data at each step.

title: Path Planning - Problem Setup
summary: Find the shortest path from S to F on an 8x8 grid with obstacles (black cells), introducing algorithmic problem-solving.
main_text: Path Planning: Find shortest path from S to F. An 8x8 grid is shown with S (Start) at position (2,3) and F (Finish) at position (5,3). Black obstacle cells block the path at positions (3,2), (3,3), and (3,4). Students must find the shortest route from S to F while avoiding obstacles.
notes_text: This path planning exercise is an extended example that runs through multiple slides. It illustrates how a computer, constrained by Fact 2 (processing one or two values at a time), must systematically explore a grid to find a path -- motivating the need for algorithms.

images.description: 8x8 grid with labeled columns 0-7 and rows 0-7, showing S at (2,3), F at (5,3), and three black obstacle cells forming an L-shape

title: Path Planning - Solution Path
summary: Shows the shortest path found from S to F by going up and around the obstacles, with explored cells highlighted in blue.
main_text: Find shortest path from S to F. The solution shows cells explored (highlighted in cyan/blue) going upward from S, around the top of the obstacle, and then down to F. The explored path includes cells at row 1 (columns 2-5), row 2 (columns 2 and 5), forming a route that navigates above the L-shaped obstacle.
notes_text: The blue cells show the exploration pattern. Notice the path goes up and around the obstacle rather than trying to go through it. This demonstrates that finding a shortest path often requires exploring multiple directions.

images.description: Same 8x8 grid with cyan/blue highlighted cells showing the explored path from S to F going up and around the black obstacles

title: Path Planning - Computer's Limited View
summary: A computer can only see one or two squares at a time, so it cannot just compute a straight line -- it might try to go straight and hit an obstacle.
main_text: Let's say you are a maps application and must find the appropriate path. Fact 2 (from earlier): A computer usually can only process (or 'see') one or two data items (a square) at a time. The slide shows the same grid but darkened so only S and F are visible -- the computer cannot see the entire grid at once. It may just compute a straight line path from S to F, unaware of obstacles.
notes_text: This is the key insight: unlike humans who can visually scan an entire map, a computer algorithm must explore the grid systematically because it can only examine one cell at a time. This constraint is what makes pathfinding algorithms necessary.

images.description: Darkened 8x8 grid where only S and F positions are visible, illustrating the computer's inability to see the whole grid at once, with text noting it may try a straight line path

title: Path Planning - Hitting an Obstacle
summary: When the computer tries to go straight from S toward F, it hits an obstacle and must find an alternative path.
main_text: The computer starts at S and moves right one cell (highlighted blue). It then encounters the obstacle (black cell with a 'no' symbol), blocking the straight path. The computer must now figure out how to navigate around this blockage.
notes_text: This shows why naive approaches fail. A simple 'go straight' algorithm breaks when obstacles are encountered. More sophisticated algorithms are needed that can explore alternatives and backtrack.

images.description: 8x8 grid showing S with one blue explored cell to its right, then a black obstacle cell with a prohibition symbol, and F further to the right

title: Path Planning - Exploring Around Obstacle
summary: After hitting an obstacle, the computer explores upward around it, with explored cells shown in blue, finding a path to F.
main_text: After being blocked, the computer explores alternative cells. Blue/cyan cells show the exploration pattern going upward from the blocked position, across the top of the obstacle, and reaching F. The grid shows the same exploration pattern as slide 37 with cells at row 1 explored across columns 2-5.
notes_text: The exploration pattern shows that the computer must try multiple directions when blocked. This systematic exploration is the basis for search algorithms like breadth-first search and depth-first search, which are formally covered in later CS courses.

images.description: 8x8 grid showing blue explored cells forming a path up and around the L-shaped obstacle from S to reach F

title: Path Planning - Unknown Finish Location
summary: When the finish location is unknown, you must examine squares one at a time in some order; asks students what order to examine them.
main_text: What if I don't know where the Finish square is? You can examine any square in any order (no longer a robot) one at a time. In what order would you examine the locations to find the shortest path to the goal location? The slide shows two grids side by side: the original with S, F, and obstacles, and a darkened version with only S visible and question marks at various locations, asking students to determine the optimal exploration order.
notes_text: This introduces the concept of uninformed search: when you don't know where the goal is, you need a systematic strategy for exploration. The question of optimal exploration order leads directly to breadth-first search.

images.description: Two grids side by side: left showing the full grid with obstacles, right showing a darkened grid where only S is visible with question marks at various positions

title: Path Planning - Breadth-First Search
summary: To find the shortest path when the goal is unknown, examine all closer locations before further ones -- this is breadth-first search.
main_text: Examine all closer squares one at a time before progressing to further squares. The grid shows numbered distances from S: cells at distance 1 (adjacent to S) are labeled '1', distance 2 labeled '2', distance 3 labeled '3'. Cells are color-coded: green for distance 1, yellow for distance 2, orange for distance 3. F is found at distance 3 from S. If you don't know where F is and want to find the shortest path, you should examine all closer locations before examining further-away locations. This uninformed search strategy for finding the shortest path is called Breadth-first search.
notes_text: Breadth-first search (BFS) is one of the fundamental algorithms in computer science. By exploring all cells at distance k before any cells at distance k+1, BFS guarantees finding the shortest path. The visual with distance numbers makes the concentric exploration pattern clear.

images.description: 8x8 grid with cells numbered by Manhattan distance from S (1, 2, 3), color-coded green (1), yellow (2), orange (3), showing the breadth-first exploration pattern with F found at distance 3

title: Overview of C++ Program Structure and Compilation - Section Divider
summary: Section divider transitioning to a high-level overview of C++ program structure and the compilation process.
main_text: A quick high-level view before we dive into the details. Overview of C++ Program Structure and Compilation.
notes_text: Transition from algorithmic thinking concepts to practical C++ programming mechanics. This section provides the first look at actual C++ code structure.

title: Coming From Other Languages - Java, Python, C++ Comparison
summary: Side-by-side comparison of the same Hello program in Java, Python, and C++ showing syntax differences and similarities.
main_text: The same program is shown in three languages. Java: import java.lang.Math.*; class Hello with public static void main(String[] args), uses System.out.println for output. Python: import math, def main(), uses print() for output, with if __name__ == "__main__": main() entry point. C++: #include <iostream> and #include <cmath>, using namespace std, void printName(string name) function, int main() entry point, uses cout << for output. All three produce the same output: Hello: Tommy Trojan, Tina Trojan, e is 2.71828. Compilation/execution differs: Java uses javac then java, Python uses python3, C++ uses g++ then ./hello.
notes_text: This comparison slide helps students transitioning from Java or Python see the parallels in C++. Key C++ differences include: explicit #include directives instead of import, cout instead of print/println, explicit return type for main, and a separate compilation step.

images.description: Three yellow code boxes side by side showing the same Hello program in Java, Python, and C++, with terminal output below each showing identical results

title: C/C++ Program Format and Structure
summary: C++ programs have comments, compiler directives (#include, using namespace), a main() function as entry point, and other functions enclosed in curly braces.
main_text: Comments: C-Style uses /* */ for multi-line comments. C++ Style uses // for single-line comments. Compiler Directives: #includes tell the compiler what other library functions you plan on using. 'using namespace std;' -- Just do it for now! main() function: Starting point of execution for the program. All code/statements in C/C++ must be inside a function. Statements execute sequentially (one line after the next) and end with a semicolon (;). Ends with a 'return 0;' statement. Other functions: Functions (and later, classes) are the primary unit of code organization (and problem decomposition/abstraction). Enclosed by { and } (aka curly braces). The code example shows: #include <iostream> for cout and endl, #include <cmath> for exp, using namespace std, a printName function, and main() calling printName and computing e.
notes_text: This is the first detailed breakdown of C++ program structure. Key points students must internalize: every program needs main(), all code lives in functions, statements end with semicolons, and #include is needed for library access. The compilation command g++ hello.cpp -o hello and execution ./hello are shown in a terminal box.

images.description: Annotated C++ code example with color-coded sections: green comments at top, blue #include directives, cyan using namespace, yellow printName function, and main function, with terminal compilation/output shown

title: Compilation and Execution Process
summary: C++ source code is compiled by g++ into an executable binary, then loaded into memory and run by the processor; three-step workflow: edit, compile, execute.
main_text: The compilation and execution pipeline: C++ file(s) (test.cpp) are fed into the g++ Compiler along with Std C++ and Other Libraries. The compiler produces an Executable Binary Image (named 'test') containing machine code (shown as binary numbers). This executable is then loaded into RAM and executed by the processor (Load and Execute). Compiler flags: -g = Enable Debugging, -Wall = Show all warnings, -o test = Specify Output executable name. Commands: $ g++ -g -Wall test.cpp -o test (compile), $ ./test (execute). The three-step development workflow is: 1. Edit and write code, 2. Compile and fix compiler errors, 3. Load and run the executable program.
notes_text: This is the fundamental development cycle for compiled languages. Unlike Python (interpreted), C++ requires an explicit compilation step that translates human-readable source code into machine-executable binary. The -g and -Wall flags should always be used during development for debugging support and warning detection.

images.description: Flowchart showing the compilation pipeline: C++ source code box -> g++ compiler (with library input from above) -> binary executable -> processor/RAM for execution, with terminal commands shown below

title: Backup - Section Divider
summary: Section divider indicating the start of backup/supplementary slides.
main_text: Backup. This section divider marks the beginning of supplementary backup slides that provide additional examples and detail.
notes_text: Backup slides contain supplementary material that may be covered if time permits or used for self-study.

title: Path Planning - Informed Search with Manhattan Distance
summary: When the finish location is known, Manhattan distance heuristic guides exploration by selecting the square with minimum estimated distance to F.
main_text: You can't see obstacles until you are directly neighboring them. Now I tell you where the finish, F, location is. Can that help you reduce the number of squares explored? The Manhattan distance formula is used: from (2,2) to (3,6), distance = |2-3| + |2-6| = 5. The grid shows S at (2,3) and F at (5,3) with distance values computed for neighboring cells: cells adjacent to S are labeled with their Manhattan distance to F (values of 3 and 5). The strategy is to select a square to explore with minimum distance to the finish.
notes_text: This introduces informed search (heuristic search). By using the Manhattan distance as a heuristic to estimate how far each cell is from the goal, we can prioritize exploring cells that appear closer to F. This is the basis for algorithms like A* search.

images.description: 8x8 grid with S and F positions, neighboring cells of S labeled with Manhattan distance values to F, and a formula showing distance calculation |2-3|+|2-6|=5

title: Path Planning - Informed Search Exploration
summary: Informed search explores cells with lowest Manhattan distance first, expanding from S toward F; red cells mark obstacles discovered during exploration.
main_text: You can't see obstacles until you are directly neighboring them. Now I tell you where the finish, F, location is. Can that help you reduce the number of squares explored? The grid shows exploration in progress: cells around S are labeled with Manhattan distances (5, 4, 3, 2). The cell with distance 2 (at position (4,3)) is selected (highlighted yellow) as it has the minimum distance to F. Red cells indicate obstacles that were discovered. Black cells are the known obstacle positions.
notes_text: The yellow cell represents the current best candidate for exploration. The red cell at (2,2) with distance 5 was explored and found to be blocked. This demonstrates how informed search prioritizes cells closer to the goal while handling obstacles discovered during exploration.

images.description: 8x8 grid with distance-labeled cells around S, yellow highlighting on the cell with minimum distance (2), red cells marking discovered obstacles, and black cells for known obstacles

title: Path Planning - Handling Blockage in Informed Search
summary: When the best-distance path is blocked, informed search picks the next-best among remaining unchosen cells to continue toward the goal.
main_text: But what if we run into a blockage? Now we would pick the best among the remaining, unchosen locations. The grid shows the same state as slide 49 with the path blocked by obstacles at (3,2)-(3,4). The cell at (4,3) with distance 2 was selected but the direct path is blocked. The algorithm now evaluates remaining yellow candidate cells and picks the one with the smallest Manhattan distance to F.
notes_text: This demonstrates the backtracking behavior of informed search. When the greedy choice leads to a dead end, the algorithm falls back to the next-best unexplored cell. This is a simplified version of how A* handles obstacles.

images.description: 8x8 grid with blocked path shown, remaining candidate cells highlighted in yellow with their distance values, demonstrating selection of next-best cell

title: Path Planning - Expanding Search After Blockage
summary: After blockage, the search expands to explore more cells, selecting from all unchosen candidates the one with minimum distance to the finish.
main_text: But what if we run into a blockage? Now we would pick the best among the remainder. The grid now shows expanded exploration with more distance-labeled cells: row 1 has values (5, 4, 3, 2), row 2 has (5, 4 with obstacle, and 1), row 3 has (5, S, 3, 2), row 4 has (5, 4), row 5 has (5). The cell at (5,2) with distance 1 is the closest to F and would be selected next. Yellow cells indicate candidates for exploration.
notes_text: Shows how the search frontier expands as blocked paths force exploration of more cells. Despite the obstacle, the informed search still explores far fewer cells than breadth-first search would, demonstrating the efficiency gained from using a distance heuristic.

images.description: 8x8 grid with expanded yellow candidate cells labeled with Manhattan distances, showing the search spreading out to find a path around obstacles to reach F at distance 1

title: Programming vs. Algorithms
summary: Programming converts an algorithm into a specific process a computer can execute; the path planning grid must be represented as numbers in memory.
main_text: Programming entails converting an algorithm into a specific process that a computer can execute. The slide shows the completed path planning grid alongside a memory diagram. The grid state (with explored cells, obstacles, distances) must be encoded as numbers stored in RAM memory addresses. The memory diagram shows addresses 0-1023 with binary values, illustrating how the abstract grid representation becomes concrete data in computer memory.
notes_text: This slide ties together the entire Unit 0 narrative: the abstract algorithm (search) must be expressed in a programming language, which the computer executes by reading and writing numbers in memory. This is the bridge from algorithmic thinking to actual C++ programming.

images.description: Path planning grid with completed search (blue explored cell, red/yellow cells, black obstacles) next to a memory diagram showing addresses 0-1023 with binary values, connecting the abstract algorithm to concrete memory storage

title: Another Example: Image Compression
summary: Images are 2-D arrays of numbers where each number is a pixel color value; image formats store these numbers in various compressed ways.
main_text: Images are just 2-D arrays (matrices) of numbers. Each number corresponds to the color or a pixel in that location. Image store those numbers in some way. The slide shows a grayscale portrait photograph with a zoomed-in section revealing individual pixels mapped to a grid of numerical values: rows of values like [0,0,0,0], [64,64,64,0], [128,192,192,0], [192,192,128,64]. These demonstrate how visual content is stored as a matrix of numbers.
notes_text: This connects back to Fact 1 (everything is a number) and introduces the concept of image compression. The pixel grid shows how even complex visual information reduces to a 2D array of integers, setting up the compression discussion on following slides.

images.description: Grayscale portrait with zoomed-in pixel grid showing numerical values for each pixel, connected by an arrow demonstrating that images are matrices of numbers

title: Example 2 and 3 - Circle and Image Representation
summary: Computers represent shapes like circles as coordinate pairs or radius/origin, and images as pixel grids; both require visiting each location individually.
main_text: A circle can be represented by the computer in different ways. As coordinate pairs of each pixel: (x,y)=(56,103), (x,y)=(57,102), (x,y)=(59,101), (x,y)=(60,100). Or as a mathematical formula: r = 120; origin = (10, 14). The computer has to enumerate and visit each location and color it black. Similarly, images are represented as grids of pixel values that must be processed one at a time.
notes_text: Shows two different representations of the same shape (coordinate list vs parametric formula). The key insight is that regardless of representation, the computer must iterate through and process each pixel individually to render the circle -- another application of Fact 2.

images.description: Circle shape shown as a smooth curve with pixelated edge detail and coordinate pairs listed, alongside the grayscale portrait pixel grid, demonstrating two types of numerical representation

title: Image Compression - Raw Pixel Data
summary: A beach photo's raw pixel data shows nearby pixels have very similar values, suggesting redundancy that can be exploited for compression.
main_text: A beach photograph is shown alongside its raw pixel data in a grid. The pixel values for the sky region are very similar: rows of values like [129, 131, 130, 133, 132, 132, 130, 129, 128, 130, 131, 129] and [130, 130, 131, 129, 131, 132, 131, 133, 130, 129, 129, 131]. Lower rows show increasing values for the sand region: [153, 155], [154, 152], [207, 204], [208, 205]. The similarity of adjacent pixel values in each region demonstrates the redundancy that compression algorithms can exploit.
notes_text: The raw data reveals that natural images have high spatial redundancy: neighboring pixels tend to have very similar values. This observation is the foundation of lossy image compression techniques like JPEG.

images.description: Beach photograph with sand and sky, alongside a large table of raw pixel values showing similar numbers within regions (sky ~129-133, sand ~152-208)

title: Image Compression - Difference Encoding and Quantization
summary: Compression works by: 1) breaking image into blocks, 2) storing differences from a reference pixel, 3) rounding differences to save space.
main_text: Image compression process: Step 1: Break image into small blocks of pixels. A 4x4 block shows values [129,131,130,133], [130,130,131,129], [132,131,130,132], [134,132,131,132]. Step 2: Store the difference of each pixel and the upper left (or some other representative pixel). The difference block becomes [129,2,1,4], [2,1,2,0], [3,2,1,3], [5,3,2,3] where 129 is the reference value and all others are small differences. Step 3: We can save more space by rounding numbers to a smaller set of options (i.e. only even number differences). The quantized block becomes [129,2,0,4], [2,0,2,0], [2,2,0,2], [4,2,2,2]. This rounding is lossy compression -- some information is lost but the numbers require fewer bits to store.
notes_text: This is a simplified explanation of how JPEG-like compression works. The key algorithmic steps are: spatial blocking, differential encoding (which produces small numbers), and quantization (which rounds those small numbers for further savings). This is lossy because quantization discards information that cannot be recovered.

images.description: Three-step compression diagram: original pixel block -> difference-encoded block -> quantized block, with beach photo and raw pixel data shown above

title: Video Compression
summary: Video is a sequence of frames at 24-30 fps; compression stores key frames and only differences between consecutive frames.
main_text: Video is a sequence of still frames at 24-30 frames per second (fps). How much difference is expected between frames? Very little, since consecutive frames are nearly identical. Idea: Store 1 of every K frames fully, with other K-1 frames being differences from frame 1 or from the previous frame. The slide shows three consecutive beach video frames with red dotted boxes highlighting the area of change (a moving object), while the background (sky and sand) remains essentially identical across frames.
notes_text: This extends image compression to the temporal domain. Video codecs like H.264/H.265 use this exact principle: I-frames (key frames) store complete images, while P-frames and B-frames store only differences from reference frames. This achieves dramatic compression ratios because most of a video frame is static background.

images.description: Three consecutive video frames of a beach scene with a moving person, red dotted boxes highlighting the changing area between frames, plus a film strip icon

title: Quotes from Bjarne Stroustrup
summary: Two famous quotes from C++ creator Bjarne Stroustrup about programming languages and the purpose of C++.
main_text: "There are only two kinds of languages: the ones people complain about and the ones nobody uses." "C++ is designed to allow you to express ideas, but if you don't have ideas or don't have any clue about how to express them, C++ doesn't offer much help." - Bjarne Stroustrup.
notes_text: These quotes from the creator of C++ encapsulate its philosophy. The first quote acknowledges that popular languages always receive criticism. The second emphasizes that C++ is a tool for expressing computational ideas -- it empowers skilled programmers but requires understanding of both the problem and the language to be effective.

images.description: Photo of Bjarne Stroustrup, creator of C++, shown below his two famous quotes in a gray text box

title: Memory Operations - High Level Operation x=x+1
summary: The high-level operation x=x+1 requires three memory steps: read x from memory, add 1 in the processor, write the new value back.
main_text: Memory (RAM) is a set of cells that each store a group of bits (usually, 1 byte = 8 bits). Each cell is referenced via a unique address. Processor can access 1 location at a time, either reading or writing that location. Read: retrieves data value in a particular location (specified using the address). Write: changes data in a location to a new value. High level operation: x=x+1. Step 1: Read x's current value from memory to the processor. The processor sends address 2 (00000010) with Read control and receives data 5 (00000101) -- the current value of x stored at address 2. Step 2: Add 1 (5+1=6). Step 3: Write x's new value (6 = 00000110) back to memory at address 2.
notes_text: This extended example of memory operations shows that even the simple statement x=x+1 involves a Read-Modify-Write cycle: (1) fetch the current value from RAM, (2) perform the arithmetic in the processor, (3) store the result back. This three-step process is fundamental to understanding how all variable manipulation works at the hardware level.

images.description: Two diagrams showing the read and write phases of x=x+1: Read operation fetches value 5 from address 2, then Write operation stores value 6 back to address 2, with full memory state shown

title: High Level Languages - Mother Tongues Timeline
summary: A comprehensive timeline chart showing the evolution of programming languages from the 1950s to 2000s, tracing the roots and relationships of computer languages.
main_text: High Level Languages: Mother Tongues -- Tracing the roots of computer languages through the ages. This comprehensive timeline chart spans from the mid-1950s to the early 2000s, showing over 50 programming languages and their evolutionary relationships. Languages are connected by lines showing influence and derivation. Key language families include: Fortran (1957) leading to later scientific languages, LISP (1958) spawning functional programming, COBOL for business applications, BASIC for education, C (1972) leading to C++ and Objective-C, Pascal and its descendants, and modern languages like Java, Python, and JavaScript. A sidebar titled 'Survival of the Fittest' explains why certain languages endure: Appeals to a wide audience (C), Gets a job done (Cobol), Delivers new functionality (Java), Fills a niche (Mathematica), Offers elegance (Icon), Has a powerful backer (C#), Has a charismatic leader (Perl).
notes_text: This timeline provides historical context for why so many programming languages exist and how they influenced each other. C and C++ sit at a critical junction point in this evolution, which is why understanding them provides insight into many other languages. The 'Survival of the Fittest' criteria explain the practical and sociological factors that determine which languages persist.

images.description: Large detailed timeline chart spanning 1954-2001 showing programming language evolution with colored bars and connecting lines between languages, plus a 'Survival of the Fittest' sidebar
